name: John Branch
one_line: A Pulitzer-winning New York Times reporter who turned the least glamorous corners of sports — the enforcer, the rodeo family, the avalanche, the winless team — into some of the most admired narrative nonfiction in American journalism.
bio: Born in Redondo Beach, California in 1967 and raised in Golden, Colorado, Branch took an unlikely route into journalism: a business degree, a stint managing a Costco, then a master's in journalism from the University of Colorado Boulder in 1996. He reported for The Gazette in Colorado Springs (starting on the business desk), became a sports columnist at The Fresno Bee, and joined The New York Times in September 2005, where he has covered sports and, increasingly, California. He was a 2011 Pulitzer finalist for 'Punched Out,' a three-part series on the death of NHL enforcer Derek Boogaard, and won the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing for 'Snow Fall: The Avalanche at Tunnel Creek' — a story whose immersive digital presentation became so influential that 'to snowfall' briefly entered newsroom slang. He has written three books — Boy on Ice (2014), The Last Cowboys (2018) and the collection Sidecountry (2021) — and lives near San Francisco.
known_for: 'Snow Fall: The Avalanche at Tunnel Creek' (2012), the Pulitzer-winning avalanche narrative that became the template for digital longform storytelling
'Punched Out' (2011), the NYT series on Derek Boogaard's death, painkillers and brain trauma in hockey
Boy on Ice: The Life and Death of Derek Boogaard (2014), winner of the PEN/ESPN Award for Literary Sports Writing
The Last Cowboys: A Pioneer Family in the New West (2018), about the Wright rodeo-and-ranching family of southern Utah
Sidecountry (2021), twenty of his favorite pieces from more than 2,000 published in the Times
'Dawn Wall' (Tommy Caldwell and Kevin Jorgeson on El Capitan) and 'Deliverance from 27,000 Feet,' on the bodies left on Everest
A body of work on the offbeat margins of sport: alligator hunters, wingsuit flyers, ultrarunners, a winless girls' basketball team, a coach rebuilding a tornado-flattened Iowa town
school: Literary/narrative nonfiction in the American magazine tradition — immersive, scene-built, reported-out feature writing, applied to the sports beat rather than to politics or war.
lineage: He works downstream of the mid-century sportswriting literary line (W.C. Heinz, Red Smith) and its late-century magazine heirs — Gary Smith at Sports Illustrated, Richard Ben Cramer, Buzz Bissinger's Friday Night Lights — plus the ordinary-people portraiture of Susan Orlean (who blurbed him) and the mountain-and-mortality reportage of Jon Krakauer. His Western books sit in the nonfiction tradition of Stegner, Ian Frazier and Timothy Egan. Downstream, 'Snow Fall' is arguably the single most imitated piece of digital journalism of the 2010s: it licensed a decade of scroll-driven multimedia projects across the Times, the Guardian, SB Nation and beyond, and helped make immersive visual storytelling a permanent newsroom function.
stance: Sport is not the subject; it is the doorway. Branch's working argument is that the interesting story is almost never the score or the star — it is the ordinary person at the edge of the game, and what their risk, obsession or death reveals about how the rest of us live. Institutions (the NHL, the rodeo economy, the ski industry, the market for spectacle) extract from these people and rarely account for the damage; the reporter's job is not to editorialize about that but to report it so thoroughly and render it so intimately that the reader cannot look away from the human cost.
blind_spots: He is a reporter, not an arguer: there is no system of thought here, and readers looking for analysis rather than portraiture will find the books thin on structural explanation — Boy on Ice indicts hockey culture largely by implication, and leans on CTE findings whose causal certainty remains scientifically contested. Gathered in one volume, the method's formula shows: a death or near-death, a small town, a lovingly observed obsessive, an elegiac close — a recipe that can shade into tragedy as aesthetic and into sentimentality. His subjects skew heavily toward rural, white, male Americana, and the empathy he extends to ranchers, hunters and fighters sometimes stops short of interrogating their politics or their choices (critics of The Last Cowboys read it as romanticizing a West whose land-use and water fights it declines to adjudicate). And 'Snow Fall' carries a legacy problem not of his making: much of the industry took the wrong lesson, mistaking parallax scrolling for narrative ambition — a confusion Branch himself has consistently pushed back on.
politics: Not genuinely discernible from the public record, and honest to say so. He is a career staff reporter at the Times who works within its no-advocacy conventions, does not write opinion columns, and has left essentially no trail of partisan commentary. His subject choices show a consistent, non-condescending sympathy for gun-owning, hunting, rodeo, Mormon-ranching and blue-collar rural America — which reads as temperamentally populist and anti-elitist in taste rather than as a party allegiance — alongside an instinct for institutional accountability (the NHL's handling of painkillers and brain injury) that reads as reformist. The Last Cowboys engages public-lands and drought politics without endorsing sagebrush-rebellion positions. Anyone assigning him a left or right label is inferring from vibes; the record does not support it.
public_views: That 'Snow Fall' worked because of the reporting and the story, not the technology — he has repeatedly deflected the multimedia credit to the Times' graphics and design teams and warned against treating the form as the achievement

That hockey's fighting culture is deeply entrenched and hard to dislodge, and that the enforcer role is corrosive to the men who fill it — a point he makes as reportage rather than as a call to ban fighting
That professional leagues were slow and incurious about the intersection of painkiller prescribing, addiction and repetitive brain trauma
That the richest material in sports lies at the margins — the 'sidecountry' — rather than in the leagues and stars that absorb most coverage
That writing about the dead carries obligations to the living: patience with families, transparency about what you're doing, and resistance to easy narrative resolution
That the ethics of risk sports are genuinely ambiguous — he presents the skiers, climbers and BASE jumpers as neither reckless fools nor heroes
That time, access and shoe-leather — years with a family, in Utah, on a mountain — are the non-negotiable ingredients, an implicit rebuke to hot-take and volume-driven sports media
interview_notes: Low-key, unpretentious and craft-focused; the opposite of a personality journalist. In radio interviews (NPR, CBC) and on journalism-craft panels he talks in concrete reporting detail — who he called, how long he stayed, what he saw — and steers away from grand pronouncements or moralizing about hockey or the West. He is notably generous about collaborators and visibly uncomfortable being credited as the inventor of a digital form. Recurring themes: patience, listening, the responsibility owed to grieving families, and a mild self-deprecation about his own unlikely path (business major, Costco manager, late arrival to journalism). He is more likely to say a story is complicated than to tell you what to conclude.
personal: Californian by birth, Coloradan by upbringing — Golden, at the edge of the Front Range — which is the origin of the mountain, snow and Western material that runs through his work. He came to journalism late and sideways after a business degree and a management job at Costco, taking his master's at CU Boulder at 28 or 29; that outsider's route shows up in his instinctive attention to working people rather than to elites. He now lives near San Francisco and covers California as well as sports; a couple of the pieces he chose for Sidecountry are personal rather than assigned, an unusual concession from a writer who otherwise keeps himself out of the frame.
key_topics: brain trauma, CTE and violence in hockey
digital storytelling and the 'Snow Fall' effect
the American West: ranching, rodeo, drought, land use
risk, adventure and mortality (avalanches, climbing, Everest)
addiction and painkillers in professional sport
